prompt.text: Write a 60-line markdown document about tides, including a 5-row table, then reply FINISHED.

rawInput.content:
# Understanding Tides

## Introduction

Tides are the rise and fall of sea levels caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on Earth's oceans. These predictable phenomena have fascinated humans for thousands of years and continue to play a crucial role in marine ecosystems, coastal navigation, and renewable energy generation.

## The Lunar Influence

The Moon is the primary force behind Earth's tides, despite being much smaller than the Sun. This is because the Moon is significantly closer to Earth than the Sun, and gravitational force decreases with distance. As the Moon orbits Earth, its gravity pulls on our oceans, creating bulges on the side facing the Moon and on the opposite side of the planet.

## Spring and Neap Tides

Tides vary in their magnitude throughout the lunar month. When the Sun and Moon align, their gravitational forces combine to create higher highs and lower lows—these are called spring tides. Conversely, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other, their gravitational effects partially cancel out, resulting in smaller tidal ranges known as neap tides.

## Tidal Cycles

Most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides each day, a pattern known as semi-diurnal tides. However, some regions experience only one high tide and one low tide daily (diurnal tides), or a mixed pattern. These variations depend on the local geography and latitude.

| Tide Type | Frequency | Characteristics | Caused By | Location |
|-----------|-----------|-----------------|-----------|----------|
| Spring Tide | Bi-weekly | Largest tidal range | Sun and Moon aligned | Global |
| Neap Tide | Bi-weekly | Smallest tidal range | Sun and Moon perpendicular | Global |
| Semidiurnal | Daily | Two high, two low tides | Moon's orbit | Atlantic Coast |
| Diurnal | Daily | One high, one low tide | Geographic factors | Gulf of Mexico |
| King Tide | Seasonal | Highest high tides | Earth at perihelion | Coastal areas |

## Practical Applications

Tides have numerous practical applications for human civilization. Fishermen use tidal charts to plan their expeditions, knowing that certain fish species are more active during specific tidal phases. Ports and harbors must account for tidal ranges when scheduling ship movements. Some innovative communities have begun harnessing tidal energy to generate electricity, creating a renewable and predictable power source.

## Conclusion

Tides remain one of nature's most reliable and predictable phenomena, governed by the eternal dance between Earth, the Moon, and the Sun. Understanding tides helps us better appreciate our planet's dynamic systems and our place within them.

# Understanding Tides: A Comprehensive Guide

## Introduction to Tidal Phenomena

Tides are the rise and fall of sea levels caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on Earth's oceans and atmosphere. These predictable and periodic phenomena have fascinated humans for thousands of years and continue to play a crucial role in marine ecosystems, coastal navigation, commerce, and renewable energy generation.

## The Lunar Influence on Ocean Water

The Moon is the primary force behind Earth's tides, despite being much smaller than the Sun. This is because the Moon is significantly closer to Earth than the Sun is, and gravitational force decreases with the square of the distance. As the Moon orbits Earth, its gravity pulls on our oceans, creating bulges on the side facing the Moon and on the opposite side of the planet.

## Spring and Neap Tidal Variations

Tides vary in their magnitude throughout the lunar month in predictable cycles. When the Sun and Moon align in the same direction relative to Earth, their gravitational forces combine to create higher highs and lower lows—these are called spring tides. Conversely, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other, their gravitational effects partially cancel out, resulting in smaller tidal ranges known as neap tides.

## Understanding Tidal Cycles and Patterns

Most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides each day, a pattern known as semi-diurnal tides. However, some regions experience only one high tide and one low tide daily (diurnal tides), or a mixed pattern. These variations depend heavily on local geography, basin shape, latitude, and other bathymetric factors.

## Comparative Tidal Characteristics

| Tide Type | Frequency | Characteristics | Caused By | Location |
|-----------|-----------|-----------------|-----------|----------|
| Spring Tide | Bi-weekly | Largest tidal range | Sun and Moon aligned | Global |
| Neap Tide | Bi-weekly | Smallest tidal range | Sun and Moon perpendicular | Global |
| Semidiurnal | Daily | Two high, two low tides | Moon's orbital position | Atlantic Coast |
| Diurnal | Daily | One high, one low tide | Geographic and latitude factors | Gulf of Mexico |
| King Tide | Seasonal | Highest high tides | Earth at perihelion + spring tide | Coastal areas |

## Impact on Marine Life and Ecosystems

Tides create dynamic environments that shape the distribution and behavior of marine organisms. Intertidal zones—areas between high and low tide marks—host unique ecosystems adapted to periodic submersion and exposure. Fish, crustaceans, and other marine species have evolved remarkable strategies to survive in these challenging conditions.

## Human Applications and Economic Importance

Tides have numerous practical applications for human civilization and commerce. Fishermen use tidal charts to plan their expeditions, knowing that certain fish species are more active during specific tidal phases. Ports and harbors must carefully account for tidal ranges when scheduling ship movements and operations.

## Renewable Energy from Tides

Some innovative coastal communities have begun harnessing tidal energy to generate electricity. Tidal power is renewable, predictable, and sustainable—offering significant advantages over other renewable sources. Tidal generators work similarly to wind turbines but operate underwater, taking advantage of the powerful flows during tidal changes.

## Conclusion and Future Perspectives

Tides remain one of nature's most reliable and predictable phenomena, governed by the gravitational dance between Earth, the Moon, and the Sun. Understanding tides helps us better appreciate our planet's dynamic systems and develop sustainable practices for our future.

## Ancient Knowledge and Modern Science

Throughout history, many ancient civilizations understood tidal patterns and incorporated this knowledge into their maritime activities. The Greeks, Romans, and various coastal cultures developed sophisticated understanding of tidal cycles. Modern science has validated and expanded upon these observations through physics and mathematics.

## Measuring and Predicting Tides

Scientists use tide gauges and satellite data to measure tidal variations worldwide. Harmonic analysis allows them to predict tides with remarkable accuracy months or even years in advance. This predictability makes tides one of the most reliable natural phenomena that humans can forecast.

## Conclusion and Future Perspectives

Tides remain one of nature's most reliable and predictable phenomena, governed by the gravitational dance between Earth, the Moon, and the Sun. Understanding tides helps us better appreciate our planet's dynamic systems and develop sustainable practices for our future. As climate change affects our oceans, monitoring tides becomes increasingly important for understanding coastal dynamics.
